newsitem.title: SOMALIA: Freed U.S. aid worker leaves Somalia for Kenya.
newsitem.headline: Freed U.S. aid worker leaves Somalia for Kenya.

text.p: An American aid worker kidnapped by Somali gunmen in north Mogadishu left for Kenya on Wednesday after his captors said his abduction was a result of mistaken identity.

Daniel Suther, who was working for the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) was freed on Wednesday in the town of Giohar, 70 km (43 miles) north of the capital after being abducted by at least eight gunmen a day earlier.
He was driven to north Mogadishu and spoke to reporters at the office of faction leader Ali Mahdi Mohamed.
"I am safe and healthy except I am dirty and tired," said Suther, who was on contract to USAID and went to north Mogadishu to check on the food situation.
Ali Mahdi said the kidnappers were hired by a group of businessmen who said the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) owed them money. Suther was seized because they wrongly thought he worked for WFP.
Suther then boarded a WFP plane to Kenya's capital Nairobi.

On Tuesday, the gunmen disarmed Suther's two Somali guards and drove off with him and his Somali driver towards the coastal town of Uarsciek, 50 km (31 miles) northeast of the capital, security sources said.
They said Ali Mahdi, whose Abgal clan alliance controls north Mogadishu, ordered the arrest of the kidnappers and sent two "technicals", four-wheel-drive battlewagons, to Uarsciek.

Kidnappings and extortion, especially involving staff of foreign aid agencies, are common in Mogadishu, where weapons are easily available and unemployment has run high since the departure of the U.N. peacekeeping operation in March 1995.
International aid agencies pulled all foreign staff out of southern Mogadishu, controlled by forces loyal to faction leader Hussein Aideed, earlier this year, but kept some staff in north Mogadishu.
The northern part of the city was widely considered far less dangerous than the south for foreigners.
Islamic courts ruled earlier this month that foreign aid workers and journalists in north Mogadishu could not be escorted by their own armed guards.

Somali gunmen have abducted more than 20 aid workers in the last three years in disputes over money. All were freed unharmed after negotiations but several foreigners were killed in other incidents. Somalia has had no central government or authority since the fall of late dictator Mohamed Siad Barre in 1991.

The south Mogadishu-based faction led by Hussein Aideed said last Friday it would free within days a 25-year-old Australian pilot sentenced to 25 years in prison for making a forced landing in western Somalia in May.
